query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that promotes the in situ formation of a coherent, lubricious oxide tribolayer on the high-entropy alloy surface will reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) without a pre-formed or stabilized lubricious surface film.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere to develop a thin, adherent oxide layer on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Testing under ambient to moderately elevated temperatures (e.g., from room temperature up to 800 °C) in environments with controlled oxygen partial pressure that allow stable oxide formation without excessive degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent, self-healing oxide tribolayer—likely enriched in oxide-forming elements present in the alloy—that acts as a barrier between contact surfaces.
generation.mechanism: The ultrathin oxide layer reduces surface shear strength and minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding, thereby lowering the coefficient of friction and reducing wear. Its stability across a wide temperature range maintains effective lubrication under varying service conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an untreated alloy, the pre-oxidized alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction (e.g., an approximate 50% reduction) and a markedly reduced wear rate (potentially by an order of magnitude), provided the oxide film remains intact and stable throughout the temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy samples that do not undergo the pre-oxidation process, exhibiting standard friction and wear characteristics under identical testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is likely to be effective in moderately oxidizing environments but may be compromised in fully inert atmospheres (where the oxide film cannot form) or in extremely aggressive chemical environments that could rapidly degrade the oxide layer.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in friction and wear reduction and the detailed composition and stability of the oxide tribolayer require experimental validation and may vary with alloy composition and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to a controlled pre-oxidation treatment in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere to form a surface oxide layer, while keeping the other set untreated. Perform reciprocating tribological tests over a broad temperature range (from room temperature up to 800 °C) under identical loading and environmental conditions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction using a reciprocating wear tester
Wear rate measured via volume loss or mass loss
Surface characterization (e.g., X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy) to confirm the presence, composition, and coherence of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show statistically significant reductions in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate compared to the untreated samples across the tested temperature range, or if the oxide layer is found to be unstable or non-adhesive, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening.
